extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology; creative-writing teachers and advanced fiction writers
extracted.subtask_description: Using structural/actantial models to analyze or design narrative elements (actors, actants, and temporal structures) in fiction; includes selecting functional actors and choosing duration/chronology strategies. Useful for literary analysis and informed creative-writing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Select which actors must be taken into consideration and which need not be; exclude actors who have no functional part in the structures of the fabula because they do not cause or undergo functional events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors like porters and maids may act (e.g., open doors) yet not belong to the category of functional events and therefore can be left out of the analysis. An initial disregard does not imply lack of significance — it only means they do not form part of the functional category. If event analysis has been skipped, use an intuitive summary as a preliminary starting point and test later (e.g., by drawing selective samples) or ask several people to write summaries and use common elements. This explicit choice lets the analyst pursue interests while keeping to an intersubjectively understandable model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional vs non-functional actors (actor selection criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate actors who cause or undergo functional events (functional actors) from those who do not; function is the deciding factor for inclusion in actantial analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional actors participate in the fabula's structure; non-functional actors may indicate social position or spatial use but fall outside actantial analysis. Use earlier event analysis to identify functional actors; beware of circularity if summaries presuppose actor subdivisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actants as classes related to teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat classes of actors (actants) by their relation to the fabula's telos: actants are classes of actors sharing a characteristic quality tied to the narrative's aim (intention/evading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structuralist model abstracts actors into actants based on teleological relations (e.g., verbs 'to wish' and 'to fear' as abstractions of intentional connections). Use this to reflect on relations between fiction, reality, and truth; remember the model is conceived in terms of fixed relations between classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject and object (actantial slots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the subject-actant (actor who pursues an aim) and the object-actant (the aim or goal), analogous to subject and direct object in a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects can be persons or states (e.g., John – wants to marry – Mary; Julien – wants to acquire – power). Typical objects include riches, love, wisdom, etc. Though theoretically disconnected from personhood, subjects are usually persons or personified animals in practice. Use examples across genres to test applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power (sender/destinateur) and receiver (destinataire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the actant who allows or supplies the object (power) and the actant who receives the object (receiver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greimas's terms destinateur/destinataire translate as sender/receiver, but 'power' better captures non-active or abstract forces (society, fate, time). Powers may be abstract or concrete; receivers may coincide with subjects. Typologies of fabulas relate to how power is concretized (e.g., in fairy tales the power as a person such as a king). Several powers may coexist (character trait plus social structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Helper and opponent (adverbial actants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish helpers and opponents as actants related not to the object but to the function connecting subject and object; they determine circumstances under which the enterprise is brought to an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helpers and opponents function like adverbial adjuncts (owing to, notwithstanding); they are often numerous and are necessary but individually insufficient to secure the aim. Helpful heuristics: powers have authority over the whole enterprise, are often abstract, remain in background and are usually single; helpers give incidental aid, are mostly concrete, come to the fore, and are usually multiple. Reader sympathy may diverge from actantial alignment (helper might be reader-antagonistic). Examples: witnesses, a talkative concierge, social class, coughs in detective fiction, birds eating crumbs in fairy tales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical inequality and coalescence of actants
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that actantial models are based on numerical inequality: one class of actants may be represented by multiple actors or one actor may instantiate several actant-classes (coalescence), and the number of actors is unlimited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actants may merge (e.g., power merges with object; receiver merges with subject). The more a fabula is oriented to the outside world, the greater the number of actors; the more subjective the fabula, the fewer actors. Examples: conventional love story where He = subject+receiver and She = object+power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubling and anti-subject (multiple autonomous subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for fabulas that have different subjects whose aims may be in opposition (an anti-subject) or entirely independent, producing sub-fabulas or moments where lines cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An anti-subject is not an opponent: an opponent opposes incidentally, whereas an anti-subject pursues its own object and program. The presence of a separate subject can indicate sub-fabulas (e.g., children/grandchildren as autonomous subjects in some novels). Powers can also split into positive/negative actants (e.g., personal will vs social structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence (determination, possibility/power, knowledge/skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the kinds of competence a subject must have to execute a program: will/determination to act; power/possibility to act; and the knowledge or skill to execute the aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greimas's subdivision distinguishes these three aspects; critics use this to classify subjects. Examples: giants/witches/wolves as power/possibility; Tom Thumb as knowledge/skill (cleverness). In detective fiction both detective and murderer may have skill/knowledge, but the murderer typically fails (makes a mistake), distinguishing the genre. Competence can be realized or undermined by fate, serendipity, or manipulation of social power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth value of actants (appearance vs reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the fabula-internal truth of actors: whether actors are what they appear to be (true), hide their identity (secret), do not exist as actors, or appear to be what they are not (lie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth consists in the coincidence of existence and appearance. Actants and whole actantial schemes may be qualified as 'true' or 'false'; fabulas may center on secrets or lies (e.g., detective stories, spy novels). Identify liars, master figures, false heroes, invisible fairies, false clues, sudden inspirations/misgivings as truth-value phenomena influencing structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further specification via psychological relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Group and specify actors according to psychological relations (e.g., daughter–mother, father–son) and psychic instances when relevant to the frame of reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological relations are crucial in psychoanalytic or psychologically oriented criticism and can determine actor specification (e.g., oedipal dynamics explaining tragedy vs comedy). These classifications can alter interpretation and typology of fabulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further specification via ideological relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Group and specify actors according to ideological oppositions (e.g., feudalism vs liberalism, patriarchy vs feminism) that the fabula engages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideological oppositions often underlie actor relations (individual vs collective; employers vs employees; men vs women) and help define the narrative's social meaning and typology (e.g., Kafka's novels focusing on individual vs representatives of power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Further specification via other oppositions (appearance, heritage, class, age, lifestyle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that physical appearance, heritage, possessions, age, lifestyle, and past experience may form actor groupings that relate to psychological or ideological oppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such oppositions may appear non-psychological at first but often connect to ideological or psychological structures (e.g., fair vs dark, red-haired as markers). These divisions help construct typologies and distinguish superficially similar fabulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration (time span) and distinction between crisis and development
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the fabula's time span (duration) and whether the narrative is structured as a crisis (short, compressed span with a representative moment) or as development (longer period showing change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration affects genre and construction: crisis forms compress events (e.g., Little Red Riding Hood half a day) and often function as 'pregnant moments'; development covers longer spans (e.g., War and Peace) and suits biographies, Bildungsromane, travel histories. Preference for one form implies a vision of fabula and reality; both require selection and have implications for constructing significance, chronology, and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of time as a generic criterion (classical tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use unity of time as a possible genre-differential or aesthetic criterion: classical tragedy traditionally limits the fabula's time span (approximately one day and one night).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While unity of time remains specific to classical tragedy, genre conventions may prescribe time-span limits that affect plausibility and perceived genre membership. Violations (e.g., Le Cid's crowding of events) invite critical reproach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implications of duration for selection, chronology, and narrative technique (constructional consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize practical consequences of choosing crisis vs development forms: how much material to present, where to summarize or skip, and how to extend/compress time via recollections, sub-fabulas, or asides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guiding points from the text: 1a) Development may present as much material as fits and tends to be longer. 1b) Crisis restricts to brief periods and suits visual media's 'pregnant moment.' 2a/2b) Development builds global significance slowly; crisis places significance centrally. 3a) Development still requires selection (skipping, summarizing). 3b) Crisis is varied via asides and recollections (extending time span), creating sub-fabulas when minor actors become protagonists, or by referencing past/future; these techniques interact with chronology (interruption, parallelism) to shape fabula construction.
